title: Beginning, Middle, End
bigQuestion: How do you turn a small thing that happened into a story a reader can see?

story.title: The Lost Tooth, Told Three Ways
story.kicker: Jamal lost a tooth. He told it three times. Each time it got better.
paragraphs: Jamal lost a tooth at lunch. He ran to his teacher. He said, "I lost my tooth!" That was all. His teacher smiled. She said, "Tell me more. What happened first?"
So Jamal tried again. "First I bit my apple. Then my tooth felt loose. Then it fell out. Last I put it in a napkin." Now his story had a beginning, a middle and an end.
His teacher asked, "What did you see? What did you feel?" Jamal thought. "The apple was red and crunchy. My tooth wiggled like a little door. I saw a tiny drop of blood. I felt proud."
Jamal told it one more time. This time he used all of it. First, next, then, last. The red apple. The wiggle. The proud feeling. His teacher said, "Now that is a story."
story.think: Which telling did you like best? What did Jamal add each time?

lessons.title: A Beginning, a Middle, an End
lessons.mainIdea: Every story has a beginning, a middle and an end.
reading: Here is a tiny story. Mia found a kitten. She gave it milk. It fell asleep in her lap. That is the whole story. It has three parts.
The *beginning* tells who and where. Mia found a kitten. The *middle* tells what happened. She gave it milk. The *end* tells how it turned out. The kitten fell asleep.
Think of a story like a walk. You start somewhere. You go somewhere. You stop somewhere. Beginning, middle, end. Every story you tell can have all three.

words.d: the first part of a story, where it starts
the part of a story where things happen
the last part of a story, where it stops

look.title: The Story in Three Pictures
look.text: Picture one: a boy holds a kite in a field. Picture two: the kite is way up in the sky. The boy runs. Picture three: the kite is stuck in a tree. The boy laughs.
look.prompt: Which picture is the beginning? Which is the end?

check.q: What does the beginning of a story tell?
check.why: The beginning tells who is in the story and where they are.

check.q: In Mia's story, what is the middle?
check.why: The middle tells what happened. Mia gave the kitten milk.

check.q: The kitten fell asleep. Which part is that?
check.why: The end tells how the story turned out. The kitten fell asleep.

lessons.title: Draw It First
lessons.mainIdea: Drawing your story first helps you know what to write.
reading: Leo wants to write about the beach. He does not know how to start. So he draws. Sand. Waves. A crab. His dad. Now he sees his story. Now he can write it.
A *drawing* is a picture you make. You can draw before you write. Draw the beginning. Draw the middle. Draw the end. Three boxes. Three pictures.
Then look at each picture. Say what you see. Write that down. Leo wrote: I saw a crab. It ran under a rock. Dad laughed. His pictures gave him the words.

words.d: a picture you make with a pencil or crayon

look.title: Three Boxes
look.text: Look at Leo's paper. Box one: a boy and a dad walk on sand. Box two: a small crab by a rock. Box three: the dad laughs and the crab is gone. Under each box there is one line for words.
look.prompt: What words would you write under box two?

check.q: Why did Leo draw before he wrote?
choices: Drawing helped him see his story
check.why: Leo did not know how to start. His pictures showed him what to write.

check.q: How many boxes did Leo draw?
check.why: He drew three boxes: beginning, middle and end.

check.q: What do you do after you draw?
choices: Say what you see and write it
check.why: Look at each picture. Say what you see. Then write it down.

lessons.title: Something That Really Happened
lessons.mainIdea: A small moment is a short, true story about one thing that happened to you.
reading: You do not need a dragon. You do not need a spaceship. You lost a mitten. You found a worm. You rode a bus. Those are stories too. They are true. They are yours.
A *small moment* is one little thing that really happened. Not your whole day. Just one part. Not the whole trip to the zoo. Just the goat that ate your map.
Pick one small moment. Close your eyes. See it again. Where were you? Who was there? What happened? Then tell it. That is a true story.

words.d: one short, true thing that happened to you

look.title: One Slice of the Day
look.text: Ava's day: she woke up, ate toast, rode the bus, did math, had recess, went home. At recess her shoe fell in a puddle. Her sock got cold and wet. She hopped on one foot all the way inside.
look.prompt: Which part of Ava's day would make the best small moment? Why?

check.q: What is a small moment?
choices: A made-up story about a dragon
Your whole day, start to end
One short, true thing that happened
check.why: A small moment is one little thing that really happened to you.

check.q: Which one is a small moment?
choices: The goat ate my map at the zoo
A spaceship went to the moon
check.why: The goat and the map is one small, true thing that happened.

check.q: Before you tell, what should you do?
choices: Close your eyes and see it again
Ask a friend to tell it for you
check.why: Seeing the moment again helps you remember where you were and what happened.

lessons.title: First, Next, Then, Last
lessons.mainIdea: Order words like first, next, then and last show what happened in order.
reading: Read this. I put on my boots. I got in the snow. I got up. I fell down. Wait. That is mixed up. You fell, then got up. The order is wrong.
*Order words* fix it. First, I put on my boots. Next, I went out in the snow. Then, I fell down. Last, I got up. Now a reader can follow you.
First tells what came first. Next and then tell what came after. Last tells the end. Use them like stepping stones. One step. Then the next.

words.d: words like first, next, then and last that tell what came when
the way things happen, one after another

look.title: Making a Sandwich
look.text: Look at the counter. Two slices of bread. A jar of jam. A knife. Now think of the steps. Open the jar. Spread the jam. Put the bread together. Take a bite.
look.prompt: Say the steps with first, next, then and last.

check.q: Which word tells what came at the end?
check.why: Last tells the end. First tells the start.

check.q: Why do we use order words?
choices: So a reader can follow what happened
check.why: Order words show what came when. A reader can follow along.

check.q: Which sentence is in the right order?
choices: First I put on boots. Then I went out.
First I fell. Then I put on boots.
Last I woke up. First I ate.
check.why: You put on boots before you go out. That order makes sense.

lessons.title: Details a Reader Can See
lessons.mainIdea: Details tell what you saw, heard and felt so a reader can see it too.
reading: I had a dog. That is true. But you cannot see the dog. Now read this. I had a small brown dog with one floppy ear. Now you see him.
A *detail* is a small piece of what you saw. Colors. Sizes. Sounds. Smells. What did it look like? What did it sound like? How did it feel?
Add one detail at a time. The apple was red. The apple was red and crunchy. It went crack when I bit it. Each detail is a little window. The reader looks through it.

words.d: a small piece of what you saw, heard, smelled or felt

look.title: Counting Details
rows: I had a small brown dog.
I had a small brown dog with a floppy ear.
look.prompt: Which sentence helps you see the dog best? What does each new detail add?

check.q: What is a detail?
choices: A small piece of what you saw or felt
check.why: A detail is a small piece, like a color, a size or a sound.

check.q: Which sentence has more details?
choices: I had a small brown dog.
check.why: Small and brown are details. They help the reader see the dog.

check.q: Why add details?
choices: So the reader can see it too
So the story is hard to read
So you can use big words
check.why: Details are like windows. The reader looks through them and sees what you saw.

lessons.title: What I Think and Why
lessons.mainIdea: An opinion tells what you think, and a reason tells why.
reading: My favorite season is winter. That is what I think. Not everyone agrees. Some kids love summer. That is fine. What I think is called an *opinion*.
An opinion needs a *reason*. A reason tells why. My favorite season is winter because I love to sled. The word because opens the door to the reason.
Try it. Pick a favorite. A food. A color. A game. Say what you think. Then say because. Then say why. That is an opinion with a reason.

words.d: what you think or feel about something

look.title: Sam's Opinion Page
look.text: My favorite lunch is pizza. I like pizza because it is warm and cheesy. I also like it because I can eat it with my hands. Pizza day is the best day.
look.prompt: What is Sam's opinion? Find the two reasons.

check.q: Which one is an opinion?
check.why: Best is what someone thinks. Not everyone will agree. That makes it an opinion.

check.q: What word often opens the door to a reason?
check.why: Because tells the reader that a reason is coming.

check.q: Why does an opinion need a reason?
choices: So a reader knows why you think it
So it will be true for everyone
check.why: A reason tells why. It helps a reader understand your opinion.

lessons.title: A Page of True Facts
lessons.mainIdea: A fact book page teaches a reader something true about one topic.
reading: Frogs have wet skin. Frogs lay eggs in water. Baby frogs are called tadpoles. These are not opinions. They are true for everyone. They are *facts*.
A fact book page is about one *topic*. Frogs. Trucks. The moon. It gives facts a reader can learn. Start with the topic. Then write two or three true things.
Where do facts come from? From looking. From books. From people who know. If you are not sure it is true, do not write it. Check first.

words.d: something that is true for everyone
the one thing a page is about

look.title: All About Ants
look.text: Ants are insects. An ant has six legs. Ants live together in big groups. Some ants carry food that is bigger than they are. Ants are small but strong.
look.prompt: What is the topic? Name one fact you learned.

check.q: Which one is a fact?
check.why: Frogs laying eggs in water is true for everyone. Cutest and gross are opinions.

check.q: What is a topic?
choices: The one thing a page is about
check.why: The topic is what the page is about, like frogs or ants.

check.q: You are not sure a fact is true. What should you do?
check.why: A fact must be true. If you are not sure, check before you write it.

lessons.title: Fixing a Sentence
lessons.mainIdea: A sentence starts with a capital letter, has a space between words and ends with a mark.
reading: Look at this. the dogran fast. Something is wrong. Three things are wrong. Can you find them?
First, a *sentence* starts with a *capital letter*. The, not the. Second, words need spaces. Dog ran, not dogran. Third, a sentence ends with a mark. A period. A question mark. An exclamation point.
Now fix it. The dog ran fast. Capital T. Spaces. A period. Read your writing out loud. Your ears will find what your eyes miss.

words.d: a group of words that tells one whole idea
a big letter, like T or M, that starts a sentence or a name

look.title: Spot the Fixes
look.text: Here is a line from Ben's paper: my cat sat on themat. Look close. Is the first letter big? Are all the words apart? Is there a mark at the end?
look.prompt: What three things would you fix in Ben's sentence?

check.q: How does a sentence start?
check.why: A sentence starts with a capital letter, like The or My.

check.q: What is wrong with dogran?
choices: It needs a space between the words
check.why: Dog and ran are two words. They need a space between them.

check.q: Which sentence is fixed right?
check.why: It has a capital T, spaces between all words and a period at the end.

review.q: What are the three parts of a story?
review.why: Every story has a beginning, a middle and an end.

choices: So you never have to write
It helps you see your story
review.why: Pictures help you see what happened. Then the words come.

choices: The day my tooth fell out at lunch
review.why: A small moment is one short, true thing that happened to you.

review.q: Which word tells what came first?
review.why: First tells the start. Then and last come after.

review.q: Which sentence has a detail a reader can see?
choices: I saw a red bike with a bell.
review.why: Red and the bell are details. They help the reader see the bike.

review.q: Which one is an opinion, not a fact?
review.why: Best is what someone thinks. The other two are true for everyone.
